title: Slow Is How You Fly
summary: Tito has perfectly good wings, but every time he tries to fly they get tangled. A butterfly shows him the trouble isn't his wings.

scenes.text:
High up on a green mountain lived Tito, a dragon the size of a middle-sized dog, with red scales that glowed like embers whenever the sun touched them.

Tito had wings. Two short wings with golden edges, perfectly good ones.

The trouble was that he didn't fly.

Every morning his cousins launched themselves off the rocks and vanished among the clouds, looping and chasing each other and puffing out sparks of pure glee. Tito watched them from below, his tummy pressed flat against the grass.

"Are you coming today?" they shouted.

"Tomorrow," Tito answered.

And tomorrow was always tomorrow again.

One day he decided that tomorrow was over.

He climbed the highest rock, puffed out his chest the way his father did, and opened his wings.

"Come on, Tito," he told himself. "You can do it."

He thought about his left wing. He thought about his right wing. He thought about whether they should move together or one after the other, and whether it was up first or down first, and how far, and how fast.

He counted three, two, one. And he jumped.

For one second he felt the wind on his face. Then his wings got tangled in each other, and down he went the way a stone goes down.

Plop!

He landed nose-first in a bush, with a yellow flower stuck to his forehead.

From a branch, an orange butterfly had seen the whole thing.

She fluttered down to the tip of his nose.

"Here's your problem," she said. "You think too much about your wings."

"But you have to think," said Tito, pulling off the flower. "Otherwise how do you know what they're supposed to do?"

"I never think about mine," said the butterfly. "And look at me."

She rose, circled once around his head and settled back down, perfectly calm.

"Your wings already know," she said. "What they can't do is fly while you're staring at them."

Tito said nothing. That had never occurred to him.

"I'm going to teach you a trick," said the butterfly. "But you have to do everything I say."

"Everything," promised Tito.

"Close your eyes. Now breathe in through your nose, slowly, until your tummy is full."

Tito did. His tummy puffed up like a balloon.

"And let it out. Even more slowly."

Tito let it out, and two little sparks came out of his nose.

"Again."

They did it four times, five, six. Tito's heart, which had been racing like a frightened rabbit, calmed down little by little. Now it beat nice and slow.

"And now," said the butterfly, "open them, and don't take your eyes off me. Look only at me."

Tito opened his eyes and looked at the butterfly.

She drifted up and down in front of him, in no hurry at all, and he followed her with his eyes. Up. Down. Up again.

He didn't think about his left wing. He didn't think about his right. He was far too busy watching his friend.

That's why it took him a while to notice that the rock was a long way away, down below. That the flowers had turned into tiny dots of colour. That the wind was whistling in his ears.

He was flying.

A laugh burst out of him. So big that it came out full of sparks.

His cousins circled around him, calling his name. And from that day on, whenever his wings got tangled, Tito did the same thing: he breathed in deep, found something lovely to look at, and let his wings do what they had always known how to do.
